title: Association between different dietary patterns and the risk of major brain disorders: a prospective multi-cohort study
abstract: Background: While diverse dietary patterns are emerging from nutritional research, comprehensive comparisons of their effects on brain health are lacking. Furthermore, the underlying biological mechanisms through which diet influences neurological and psychiatric outcomes remain largely unclear. Methods: Using data from the UK Biobank, a large-scale prospective cohort (with participant enrolled between April, 2009, and June, 2012), we used Cox proportional hazards models to analyse the associations between ten dietary patterns (including the Mediterranean diet, the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet, and the Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND) diet, the alternative healthy eating index (AHEI), the healthful plant-based dietary index (hPDI), the planetary health diet index (PHDI), the healthy low-carbohydrate diet (HLCD), the healthy low-fat diet (HLFD), the dietary index for gut microbiota (DI-GM), and the reversed energy-adjusted diet inflammatory index (rEDII)) and ultra-processed food (UPF) intake with the incident risk of five major brain disorders, including dementia, stroke, depression, anxiety, and Parkinson's disease (PD) in participants with available dietary data who were free of major brain disorders at baseline. The most neuroprotective diet identified was then validated for its associations with a range of brain health outcomes in the U.S. Health and Retirement Study (HRS, with participant data collected between 2013 and 2014) and the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS, with participant data collected in 2018) using generalized linear models to analyze the data. Participants from these two cohorts were required to have complete data on diet, outcomes, and covariates. Finally, we employed a four-way decomposition model with multi-omics data as mediators to explore the underlying mechanisms. Findings: In the UK Biobank cohort (N = 166,916), MIND diet demonstrated the broadest neuroprotective effects. Over a median follow-up of 10·5 years, 1870 participants were diagnosed with dementia, 980 with PD, 3121 with stroke, 5113 with depression, and 5697 with anxiety. Adherence to the MIND diet was significantly associated with a reduced risk of dementia (hazard ratio [HR] = 0·87, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0·77-0·98), stroke (HR = 0·89, 95% CI = 0·81-0·98), depression (HR = 0·77, 95% CI = 0·71-0·82), and anxiety (HR = 0·82, 95% CI = 0·76-0·88), but not PD (HR = 0·94, 95% CI = 0·80-1·11). In the HRS (n = 4496) and CLHLS (n = 9099) validation cohorts, the MIND diet remained significantly associated with lower risks of depression and anxiety, as well as better cognitive performance (in HRS: better cognitive function (β = 0·78, 95% CI = 0·47-1·10), fewer depressive symptoms (β = -0·22, 95% CI = -0·39 to -0·06), and fewer anxiety symptoms (β = -0·40, 95% CI = -0·78 to -0·02); in CLHLS: lower odds of cognitive impairment (odds ratio [OR] = 0·45, 95% CI = 0·37-0·55), depression (OR = 0·44, 95% CI = 0·38-0·52), and anxiety (OR = 0·49, 95% CI = 0·41-0·60)). In contrast, the intake of UPF was associated with an increased risk for dementia (HR = 1·40, 95% CI = 1·25-1·56), PD (HR = 1·26, 95% CI = 1·08-1·47), depression (HR = 1·42, 95% CI = 1·34-1·50), and anxiety (HR = 1·26, 95% CI = 1·19-1.33) in the UK Biobank cohort. Mechanistically, multi-omics analyses revealed that the MIND diet's protective effects were mediated through several key pathways. A favourable metabolic signature explained a substantial proportion of the reduced risk for stroke (proportion mediated = 60·63%), depression (38·97%), and anxiety (26·06%). Furthermore, slower biological ageing significantly mediated the reduced risk of dementia (19·40%). A structural equation model confirmed the overall protective pathway linking the MIND diet to better brain health via these mediators. Conversely, higher UPF intake was found to increase brain disease risk through detrimental changes in these same metabolic, and ageing pathways. Interpretation: This study supports the MIND diet as a promising intervention for promoting brain health and mitigating neuropsychiatric disorders, while highlighting UPF intake as a significant modifiable risk factor. By identifying specific metabolic, inflammatory, and ageing-related biological pathways, our findings provide potential targets for future research and targeted interventions. However, these observational associations require definitive confirmation through further experimental studies, such as randomised controlled trials. title: In preprints: cell type-specific gene regulation through the lens of echinoderms
abstract: One of the most intriguing questions in developmental biology is how a single cell, the zygote, gives rise to hundreds or millions of distinct cell types during embryogenesis. Decades of research have shown that cell fate is controlled by gene regulation through activation and repression of genes, as orchestrated by cell type-specific gene regulatory networks (GRNs) (Britten and Davidson, 1969; Jacob and Monod, 1961). Multiomics-based approaches, including genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and epigenomics, have reshaped the study of gene regulation and cell fate, enabling holistic systems-level analyses. Comparative GRN studies have further revealed the evolutionary origins of cell types and developmental processes across metazoans (Arendt et al., 2016; Peter and Davidson, 2011).Echinoderms, particularly sea urchins, have been instrumental in advancing our understanding of embryonic development and cell type evolution (Arnone et al., 2016; Ernst, 2011). Sea urchins are non-chordate deuterostomes that are amenable to genetic perturbation; they show highly regulative development (Driesch, 1891) and produce millions of transparent synchronously developing embryos. Moreover, they have served as an ideal experimental system for studying the body plans and life cycle dynamics as the embryo-adult continuity is interrupted in most known species by a planktonic pluteus larva (Arnone et al., 2015). Owing to their many advantages as an experimental system, sea urchin embryos and larvae have been instrumental in understanding the principles of gene regulation and embryonic development.Importantly, sea urchins were used to reconstruct the first comprehensive developmental GRN and some of the largest known metazoan GRNs (Cary and Hinman, 2017; Davidson et al., 2002; Shashikant et al., 2018). Therefore, it is no surprise that in the multiomics era, sea urchins remain central to the evolutionary developmental biology field, as there is a strong knowledge backbone to build on. For instance, multiomics-based approaches applied on echinoderms have contributed to refining cell type-specific GRNs (Voronov et al., 2024), examining life-history evolution and reprogramming (Berrio et al., 2024; Davidson et al., 2022), identifying novel and conserved cell types (Paganos et al., 2021, 2022), mapping developmental regulatory profiles (Paganos et al., 2025 preprint; Voronov et al., 2024), exploring genomic links to longevity (Polinski et al., 2024), and studying environmental effects on developmental GRNs (Armstrong et al., 2025; O'Donnell et al., 2010; Paganos et al., 2023).In a recent preprint, Brandenburg and colleagues showcase the power of multiomics to assess cell type-specific gene regulation during the development of the sea urchin Strongylocentrotus purpuratus. They combined single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with single-cell thiol-(SH)-linked alkylation of RNA for metabolic labelling sequencing (scSLAM-seq) to profile gene expression and measure newly synthesized transcripts. Moreover, to assess gene regulation and chromatin accessibility, the authors used both whole-organism and single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (scATAC-seq). This integrative approach provides new insights into the dynamics and evolution of gene regulation, highlighting sea urchins and echinoderms as valuable systems for studying evolution and development.A crucial step in understanding transcriptomic and regulatory dynamics during embryogenesis is building high-resolution transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility atlases. To achieve this, Brandenburg and colleagues performed scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq across early S. purpuratus development, identifying 47 transcriptomic states and 37 regulatory states spanning all major developmental lineages. The high quality of the scATAC-seq data was validated by comparing it to previously characterized cis-regulatory elements (CREs), supported by decades of CRE research in sea urchins.Leveraging these atlases, the authors asked whether they could identify genes driving cell type diversification and reconstruct developmental lineage relationships. Using ancestry inference-based computational approaches, they successfully mirrored lineage trees built from scRNA-seq data (Paganos et al., 2021) and classical lineage tracing (Cameron et al., 1987), increasing confidence in their maps. For example, lineages such as skeletal cells and small micromeres were already distinguishable by the 64-cell stage.Finally, analysis of transcription factor dynamics revealed several previously unreported transcription factors (TFs) with putative roles in early development. This was the case for znf875/z193 in neurogenesis, zc4h2 in oral ectoderm and rreb1 in globular immune cells: not only were these TFs expressed in the right cell types at the right time, but their cis-regulatory elements were also specifically accessible in the respective lineages. The robustness of these findings is supported by the detection of known TFs like alx1 and foxA, with established roles in skeletal and endodermal specification, respectively. For alx1, the authors even identified novel CREs, deepening our understanding of its regulation. Strikingly, computational analyses showed that regulatory element usage is highly conserved within germ layers, and that many TFs are reused across unrelated lineages, consistent with the known pleiotropy of sea urchin TFs. These shared TFs often use distinct regulatory sites, particularly within introns, while flanking regulatory elements remain accessible across all expressing tissues, illustrating how diverse regulatory states can be orchestrated by a limited set of TFs.One fundamental question in embryonic development is the timing of the maternal to zygotic transition. Using scSLAM-seq, a method that measures the rate of transcription to detect newly synthesized RNA in individual cells, the authors found that a major wave of zygotic genome activation (ZGA) occurs at the 128-cell stage (∼10 hpf), coinciding with the documented cell type-specific transcription, loss of developmental plasticity and chromatin maturation. They also identified a subset of genes activated in the 4th cleavage stage embryo, suggesting localized regulatory activity before global ZGA. Moreover, using time-course multiomics data, the authors showed that chromatin accessibility, and thus gene regulation, progress in two phases: an early phase dominated by promoter-proximal peaks; and a later phase enriched in distal elements, accompanying cell type diversification. Additional computational correlation analyses between the generated datasets revealed a strong link between promoter accessibility and gene expression.Among the sea urchin cell types studied to date, skeletogenic cells and neurons are some of the most extensively characterized at the levels of developmental origins, molecular signature, function and GRNs. Therefore, the authors set out to investigate the diversity and development of these cell types in their datasets. The sea urchin larval skeleton is produced at the early larva stage when skeletogenic cells fuse, forming syncytial calcium carbonate rods. Skeletal cells along the rods utilize diverse GRN sub-circuits associated with distinct functions. In this study, Brandenburg and colleagues found that the skeletogenic cell states are highly diverse, with only a limited set of six transcription factors, including alx1, ets1 and mitf, shared across the skeletal subtypes. Moreover, they identified a total of 100 genes associated with calcification that showed distinct transcriptional profiles between the skeletal rod subtypes, a finding they suggest may reflect distinct spatial cues or differences in calcification modes. Additionally, comparison of differential accessible peaks between skeletogenic and oral non-skeletogenic mesoderm (NSM) cells identified a large fraction of shared peaks. Importantly, one of the shared motifs found corresponds to the transcription factor Ets1, suggesting its crucial role in both skeletogenic and NSM lineages. These data, taken together with previous studies demonstrating that NSM cells can transfate into skeletogenic cells when the skeletogenic lineage is eliminated from the early embryo, led the authors to propose that this similarity may reflect the NSM-to-skeletogenic transfating potential. Such findings constitute a paradigm on how multimodal approaches can shed light on complex regulatory mechanisms such as cell fate rewiring.The authors also investigated the regulatory and transcriptomic states of neurons, a cell type that was previously demonstrated to have diverse origins from the ectoderm (oral and apical) and the endoderm. Using sub-clustering and diffusion maps, the authors were able to define nine neuronal transcriptomic states corresponding to three distinct developmental trajectories: serotonergic, dopaminergic and ciliary band neurons. Each was defined by distinct transcription factors, such as soxC and foxN1/4 in neuronal precursors, prox1 in ciliary band neurons, fezf2 and lhx9 in serotonergic neurons, and otp and lmx1 in dopaminergic neurons. Interestingly, motif analysis revealed conservation of neurogenesis transcription factors between sea urchin, human and fruit fly, prompting the authors to suggest a possible evolutionary conservation of ectodermal neuronal programs.In summary, the preprint by Brandenburg and colleagues provides valuable new insights into the regulatory dynamics of embryonic development in a non-chordate deuterostome. It underscores the strength of echinoderms as experimental systems for addressing fundamental questions in evolutionary and developmental (Evo-Devo) biology. This study marks a milestone in demonstrating how multi-omics approaches, when applied to invertebrates, can reveal complex regulatory mechanisms that might be difficult or even impossible to uncover in other animal systems. The approaches adopted by the authors of this study align with current efforts in the Evo-Devo research field to standardize and enable omics-based comparisons across species, with the aim of tracing cell type and, thus, animal evolution (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2025). Therefore, this preprint highlights that as omics technologies continue to advance and become more accessible, echinoderms and marine invertebrates more broadly will remain indispensable systems for studying gene regulatory networks, cell type diversity and evolutionary processes.Paganos et al. title: The antiaging effect of edible bird's nest on the skin of healthy women: a randomized controlled trial
abstract: Skin is an important barrier organ of the human body. As we age, the appearance and function of our skin deteriorate, which poses health risks. The use of edible bird's nest (EBN) to nourish the skin is an ancient method in Asia. However, the role and mechanism of EBN products in improving human skin aging are still unclear. Therefore, we conducted a randomized controlled trial that included 92 healthy female volunteers aged 25–45 years. They were randomly divided into the high-dose group, the low-dose group, and the control group, and they completed a 12-week treatment. The results showed that the consumption of high-dose EBN significantly improved skin moisture and elasticity by 22.14% and 5.89%, respectively, and significantly reduced the number of deep wrinkles, light wrinkles and spot area by 18.47%, 0.64%, and 3.05%, respectively. ELISA results showed that EBN decreased the expression of inflammatory factors (IL-6 and TNF-α) and serum factors (NO, MMP-1, MMP-9). Moreover, EBN can reverse the aging-induced decreases in SOD and LOX, thus slowing down the aging process. Fecal metagenome results showed that EBN significantly increased the abundance of beneficial bacteria ( Bacteroides_uniformis and Bacteroides_finegoldii ). Serum and fecal non-target metabolomic results showed that EBN significantly increased serum and fecal metabolite (N-methylnicotinamide, 2-deoxyribose 5-phosphate, and dimethylmalonic acid) concentrations compared with the control group. Furthermore, correlation analysis revealed a positive association between N-methylnicotinamide levels and skin elasticity. These findings suggest that EBN may ameliorate skin aging by enhancing the diversity of beneficial gut bacteria and their metabolites.

title: iPSCs derived sEVs ameliorate NK cell senescence by targeting CISH-STAT3
abstract: BACKGROUND: Natural killer (NK) cells, essential components of the innate immune system, undergo subtype changes with aging that diminish their cytotoxic and tumor surveillance functions. Recent reports indicate that small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) derived from stem cells could ameliorate age-related diseases, while their effects on NK cell senescence remain unexplored. METHODS: We administered induced pluripotent stem cell(iPSC) derived sEVs via tail vein injection for 6 months to naturally aged mouse models. Then we detected a senescent phenotype of splenic NK cells based on a series recognized markers in aged mice. To further investigate the impact of iPSC-sEVs mediated rejuvenation on NK cell function in vivo, purified splenic NK cells from iPSC-sEVs or vehicle-treated mice were co-injected subcutaneously with B16 tumor cells to establish co-inoculation models. In vitro, we used D-gal induced NK92 aged model and conducted transcriptome analysis on the cells. Furthermore, NK92 cells overexpressing CISH were used to explore the mechanism by which iPSC-sEVs improve NK92 cells senescence. Further we conducted a mass spectrometry analysis of the substances in iPSC-sEVs and performed bioinformatics analysis. RESULTS: iPSC-sEVs treatment partially reversed these immunosenescence phenotypes in aged mice models. In splenic NK and B16 tumor cells co-inoculation models, iPSC-sEVs-NK cells exhibited significantly enhanced cytotoxicity against tumor cells and the ability to recruit T cells. Mechanistic studies suggest that iPSC-sEVs inhibit the upregulation of CISH in senescent NK cells, subsequently activating p-STAT3, which is involved in regulating NK cell senescence and cytotoxicity. Overexpression of CISH significantly suppresses STAT3 phosphorylation and accelerates NK92 cell senescence. Proteomic analysis indicates that iPSC-sEVs modulate the CISH-STAT3 signaling pathway by delivering RNA binding proteins. CONCLUSIONS: In summary, our study shows that iPSC-sEVs effectively rejuvenate senescent NK cells by partially suppressing CISH expression and promoting STAT3 phosphorylation. As a cell-free therapeutic agent, iPSC-sEVs represent a promising strategy for treating cancer in the elderly and other inflammatory senescence-related diseases.

title: ITTHACA: A Joint Multicenter Initiative in the Basque Country (Spain) for Biomarker, Biosensor, and Predictive Model Research for Healthy Aging based on CITA GO‐ON study, a FINGER Study
abstract: BACKGROUND: The ITTHACA project is a collaborative initiative involving six research institutions from the Basque Country including Universities, Health, Technology and Basic Research Institutions. It builds upon the ongoing CITA GO-ON) CITA Go-On study, ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04840030) cohort study, which adapts the Finnish FINGER [Ngandu, T., et al. 2015] model to the local context. ITTHACA focuses on enhancing healthy aging by identifying markers, prediction models and sensors for in vivo monitoring that allow the establishment and implementation of combined intervention strategies in the population. METHOD: This one-year randomized-controlled trial (total n = 250; 125 control and 125 intervention), focused on 60-85-year-old males and females at risk of dementia, adopts a multimodal approach. Biomarker identification includes proteomics and metabolomics in biological fluids (blood) and 16S metagenomics and lipidomics in the gut microbiome (stool), as well as employing a FINGER-like mice model. Biosensor technology under development includes multi-channel bioimpedance spectroscopy for tissue analysis and electrochemical sensors for real-time detection of aging markers in biofluids. Predictive modeling integrates data from these analyses and multiple domains-cognition, cardiovascular health, voice, food texture perception and habits-to generate diagnostic tools that monitor biological aging and inform early interventions. A proof-of-concept study in an older population sample, with special attention to user experience, will evaluate the potential benefits of these findings in improving the quality of life for older adults. RESULT: Not applicable. The ITTHACA project is ongoing, with outcomes expected to include validated biomarkers, novel biosensors, and predictive models that facilitate early interventions. CONCLUSION: ITTHACA demonstrates the power of interdisciplinary collaboration in tackling the complex multidomain challenge of aging. By leveraging the expertise of complementary Basque Country Research Centers, this initiative is poised to produce innovative resources for prolonging healthy and autonomous living. The project's outcomes are expected to support new therapeutic strategies and socio-healthcare interventions that address the rising prevalence of aging-related conditions, including cognitive decline.

title: Biomarker Insights Into Brain Health, Aging, and Healthspan
abstract: Abstract There has been a surge in the novel biomarker approach to identify early predictors of diseases, understand multiple disease etiology, and, more importantly, the effect of biological aging on health and disease dynamics. In this symposium, we will present novel biomarker data to reveal novel pathways related to brain health, dementia, and biomarker signatures of longevity and healthspan. This symposium features 5 presentations of recently conducted studies using biomarker data from US and European cohorts. First, Dr. Diniz will present recent results suggesting that a history of major depression is causally associated with biological aging acceleration using Mendelian randomization approaches. Second, Dr. Tian will present data about developing a novel biomarker composite score based on eye-movement measures and its association with age-related cognitive and mobility decline. Third, Dr. Evans uses data from the Longevity Consortium to examine metabolomic signatures of human aging and longevity. Firth, Dr. Liu shows a novel protein-based signature predictive of cumulative frailty index, the proteomic frailty index (pFI), and examines the association of pFI with multiple health indicators in three independent cohorts, including physical, clinical and cognitive measures, dementia, and mortality. Finally, Dr. Kuo will show the development of a healthspan proteomic score (HPS) to identify proteomic signatures of healthspan and its association with mortality and multiple age-related adverse health outcomes. Based on the symposium presentations, we seek to generate discussions of how biomarkers can aid the understanding of novel risk factors for accelerated biological aging, dementia risk, and healthspan.

title: NAPTICON-2025 – SYSTEMATIC REVIEWS AND META-ANALYSIS
abstract: Systematic reviews and meta-analysis: Faculty abstracts – General category Conference Code: OP-302: Efficacy of methylphenidate in adult-onset ADHD: A systematic review and meta-analysis M. Mohanalakshmi, Mohammed Gani, K. Sathish Babu, Banupriya, Rahul, J. Premalatha Department of Pharmacology, Government Medical College, Karur, Tamil Nadu, India Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in adults is associated with persistent inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity, and impaired quality of life (QoL). This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesised evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating methylphenidate (MPH) in adults (≥18 years) diagnosed per DSM/ICD criteria. Searches were conducted in PubMed, Cochrane CENTRAL, and ClinicalTrials.gov (updated July 2025). Eligible studies assessed MPH monotherapy or MPH combined with cognitive- behavioural therapy (CBT) for ≥4 weeks, reporting outcomes on ADHD symptoms, QoL, functional impairment, and safety. Standardized mean differences (SMD) were pooled using a random-effects model, and heterogeneity assessed via I² statistics. Six meta-analyses (n=1, 200 MPH; n=900 placebo) showed a pooled SMD of 0.90 (95% CI 0.65–1.15) for core symptoms with optimized dosing; non-continuous release formulations achieved SMD 0.58. Greatest improvements were observed for inattention (d=0.68), followed by hyperactivity (d=0.51) and impulsivity (d=0.46). QoL improvements were small-to-moderate (SMD 0.38). MPH+CBT yielded additional functional gains (SMD 0.30–0.45) in limited trials. Common adverse events included decreased appetite (20%), dry mouth (15%), palpitations (13%), and headache (10%); discontinuations were low (4.3%). Mechanistic evidence from animal models supports MPH’s long-term benefits via neuronal remodeling, dopamine transporter normalization, neuroglial changes, and Wnt pathway activation, without structural brain loss. Clinical Implications: Optimal non-continuous release MPH (57–72 mg/day) should be considered a first-line pharmacological option for adult ADHD, with adjunctive CBT for patients requiring additional functional improvement. Conference Code: OP-311: Revefenacin in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: A systematic review and network meta-analysis of safety and clinical efficacy Siddhartha Dutta1, Rima Shah1, Shubha Singhal1, Mamta Singh2, Sagar Dholariya3 1Department of Pharmacology, AIIMS, Rajkot, Gujarat, India, 2Department of Ophthalmology, AIIMS, Rajkot, Gujarat, India, 3Department of Biochemistry, AIIMS, Rajkot, Gujarat, India Background: Revefenacin is a novel long-acting muscarinic antagonist for maintenance therapy in COPD. This systematic review and metanalysis aimed to assess the safety and efficacy of revefenacin in COPD. Methods: The online databases like PubMed/Medline, Cochrane-library, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched until 28th August 2025 for studies comparing Revefenacin to placebo or active treatments using keywords such as “Revefenacin” and ‘COPD’. All statistical analysis were conducted with R. Posit Software and Review Manager (RevMan 5.4) software. A network meta-analysis (NMA) was conducted with frequentist methods. Results: Of the 118 titles searched; after removing duplicates, 75 studies were evaluated for eligibility. Finally, 11 RCTs were finally included. Revefenacin was compared with placebo and active control (tiotropium). A subgroup analysis was conducted based on the treatment duration. In the safety analysis, there was no significant difference between TAE [OR=0.98 (0.75, 1.29), I2=25%, p=0.91], SAE [OR=0.99 (0.60, 1.64), I2=0%, p=0.97], NSAE [OR=1.29 (0.66, 2.51), I2=85%, p=0.45] as compared to placebo, or tiotropium [TAE: OR=0.65 (0.32, 1.30), I2=82%, p=0.22], [SAE: OR=0.82 (0.57, 1.18), I2=0%, p=0.28] and [NSAE: OR=0.70 (0.35, 1.40), I2=79%, p=0.32] respectively. In NMA comparing rank of treatments, tiotropium had highest SUCRA and P scores for TAE (75%, 0.74) and SAE (65%, 0.63) followed by placebo in TAE (54%, 0.54) and revefenacin 175 in SAE (59%, 0.58). A significant change was observed with majority of efficacy parameters like change in trough FEV1 (Revefenacin vs. Placebo) [MD=145.15 (133.36, 156.94), I2=96%, p< 0.00001], MRMU [MD=-0.30 (-0.59, -0.02), I2=99%, p=0.04] and proportion of SGRQ [OR=1.58 (1.19, 2.10), I2=0%, p=0.002]. In NMA comparing rank of treatment for FEV1, tiotropium (81%, 0.85) had highest SUCRA and P scores followed by revefenacin 175 (74%, 0.76). Conclusion: This study demonstrates that revefenacin has a fair safety profile as compared to placebo or tiotropium and is more effective than placebo in therapy of COPD. Dharani Department of Pharmacology, Vinayaka Mission’s Kirupananda Variyar Medical College & Hospital, Salem, Tamil Nadu, India Introduction: The occurrence of falls creates danger for people who are older adults & those with limited mobility because it produces serious medical outcomes with extended disabilities.Current advances in real time fall detection as well as prevention systems emerged through the combination of machine learning techniques with Internet of Things devices. Objectives: The purpose of this review is to assess recent development in ML- based fall detection systems that focuses on the impact of ML models on fall detection precision, the function of IoT devices in providing wide scale invisible supervision & Emerging patterns alongside future research prospects in this field. Conclusion: The application of ML & IoT like deep learning models have become dominant in detecting falls through their implementation of CNNs, BiLSTM & Transformers resulting accuracy being reported over 97%. title: Biological Aging Acceleration in Major Depressive Disorder: A Multi‐Omics Analysis
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is linked to a higher risk of premature aging, but the mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear. Using data from two population cohorts (UK Biobank and Finnish Twin Cohort), we evaluate the relationship between systemic and organ-specific proteomic and epigenetic aging acceleration and MDD. A lifetime history of MDD was associated with accelerated proteomic aging at both systemic and organ-specific levels-including the brain-in both cohorts, with stronger associations than those observed with systemic epigenetic aging. Systemic and brain-specific proteomic aging acceleration were linked to higher risks of incident MDD and a greater risk of Alzheimer's disease, related dementia, and mortality among individuals with MDD in the UK Biobank. Evidence of depressive episode remission attenuated the association between MDD and systemic and brain-specific proteomic aging acceleration. Finally, Mendelian randomization analyses revealed a causal effect of MDD on systemic and brain-specific proteomic aging acceleration. Our results suggest a strong bidirectional association between MDD and biological aging acceleration. Biological aging acceleration, assessed by proteomic systemic and organ-specific clocks, can serve as a novel therapeutic target for treating MDD and for mitigating the long-term risks of adverse health outcomes associated with this condition.
authors: Breno S. Diniz; Shangshu Zhao; Gabin Drouard; Eero Vuoksimaa; Miina Ollikainen; Eric J. Lenze; Ming Xu; Richard H. Fortinsky; George A. Kuchel; Jaakko Kaprio; Chia‐Ling Kuo

title: Nanomedicine for Cancer and Autoimmune Immunotherapy
abstract: Nanomedicine has now become a transformative platform that enhances the precision and efficacy of immunotherapy approaches and allows customizations like never before when it comes to cancer, as well as autoimmune conditions. Using platforms based on nanoscale, researchers have been able to manipulate immune responses operating across spatial and temporal scales to address key limitations of conventional immunotherapy associated with working with immune response such as immune evasion, systemic toxicity, and poor pharmacokinetics. Sophisticated nanoparticles (such as stimuli-sensitive ones, exosome-mimetic vesicle nanoparticles, and nanoparticles with CRISPR) allow directed immunomodulators, antigens, and gene-editing systems to reach one or more particular immune compartments. The innovations allow reprogramming of immune cells, immune tolerance rejuvenation, and expansion of antitumor immunity without significant off-target effects. Finding applications in integrating the artificial intelligence as well as multi-omics techniques, the process leads to personalization of the nano-immunotherapies based on patient-specific immuno-signatures. The chapter discusses the mechanistic rationale, therapeutic advancement, and the translational opportunities of nanotechnology-based immunotherapies that define them as part of a foundation of future generations of clinical approaches to precision immune modulation in oncology and autoimmune diseases.
authors: Ashi Ramavat; Priya Antil; Soniya Kaushik; Baby Kataria; Ramendra Pati Pandey

title: In-situ glial cell-surface proteomics identifies pro-longevity factors in Drosophila
abstract: Much focus has shifted towards understanding how glial dysfunction contributes to age-related neurodegeneration due to the critical roles glial cells play in maintaining healthy brain function. Cell-cell interactions, which are largely mediated by cell-surface proteins, control many critical aspects of development and physiology; as such, dysregulation of glial cell-surface proteins in particular is hypothesized to play an important role in age-related neurodegeneration. However, it remains technically difficult to profile glial cell-surface proteins in intact brains. Here, we applied a cell-surface proteomic profiling method to glial cells from intact brains in Drosophila, which enabled us to fully profile cell-surface proteomes in-situ, preserving native cell-cell interactions that would otherwise be omitted using traditional proteomics methods. Applying this platform to young and old flies, we investigated how glial cell-surface proteomes change during aging. We identified candidate genes predicted to be involved in brain aging, including several associated with neural development and synapse wiring molecules not previously thought to be particularly active in glia. Through a functional genetic screen, we identified one surface protein, DIP-β, which is down-regulated in old flies and can increase fly lifespan when overexpressed in adult glial cells. We further performed whole-head single-nucleus RNA-seq and revealed that DIP-β overexpression mainly impacts glial and fat cells. We also found that glial DIP-β overexpression was associated with improved cell-cell communication, which may contribute to the observed lifespan extension. Our study is the first to apply in-situ cell-surface proteomics to glial cells in Drosophila, and to identify DIP-β as a potential glial regulator of brain aging.

title: Egr1 is a sex-dependent regulator of neuronal chromatin, structural plasticity, and behaviour
abstract: Sex differences are found in brain structure and function across species, and across brain disorders in humans. A major source of brain sex differences is differential secretion of steroid hormones from the gonads across the lifespan. Specifically, ovarian hormones oestrogens and progesterone are known to dynamically change structure and function of the adult female brain, having a major impact on psychiatric risk. However, due to limited molecular studies in female rodents, very little is still known about molecular drivers of female-specific brain and behavioural plasticity. Here we show that ventral hippocampal (vHIP) overexpression of Egr1, an oestrous cycle-dependent transcription factor, induces sex-dependent changes in vHIP neuronal chromatin, gene expression, and structural plasticity, along with female-specific effects on vHIP-dependent behaviours. Importantly, Egr1 overexpression and knockdown partially mimic the vHIP chromatin state associated with the high and low-oestrogenic phase of the oestrous cycle, respectively. We demonstrate that Egr1 directs neuronal chromatin opening across the sexes, although with limited genomic overlap. Our study not only reveals a sex-dependent chromatin regulator in the brain, but also provides functional evidence that this sex-dependent gene regulation drives structural and behavioural plasticity, informing sex-based treatments for brain disorders.
authors: Devin Rocks; Luisa Demarchi; Laila Ouldibbat; Eric Purisic; Heining Cham; Eduardo F. Gallo; John M. Greally; Masako Suzuki; Marija Kundaković

title: Effect of bedrest on the human gut and oral microbiome: implications for frailty
abstract: The physiological effects of spaceflight resemble those of ageing and prolonged inactivity, and ground-based microgravity analogs have emerged as promising models for studying frailty. The human microbiome is increasingly recognised for its role in age-associated decline, although precise mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we evaluate the gut and oral microbiomes of twenty-two participants, aged 55-65, who were enrolled in a head-down tilt bedrest (HDBR) study, the first Canadian HDBR study conducted in an older cohort. Participants were randomly assigned to an inactivity or multi-modality exercise intervention group for fourteen days of HDBR, followed by seven days of rehabilitation and additional follow-up appointments. Gut (n=343) and oral (n=344) taxonomic profiles were generated using V4/V5 16S rRNA gene sequencing from fecal and salivary samples collected throughout the study. Gut functional profiles were generated using metagenomic (n=86) and metabolomic (n=83) data. Frailty was measured using a 36-item frailty index. Inactivity-associated changes to the gut microbiome during HDBR included decreasing α-diversity, decreasing Akkermansia and Lactobacillus , and increasing Bacteroides . Exercise-associated changes included increasing gut Roseburia . Interestingly, oral microbiome β-diversity was more strongly associated with frailty than the gut. We conclude that inactivity-associated changes to the human microbiome could contribute to the early stages of frailty development, and that exercise can serve as an effective countermeasure against these effects. These results may inform strategies to preserve the health of both older adults facing prolonged periods of inactivity, as well as astronauts during longer space exploration missions
authors: Monica Alvaro-Fuss; Vanessa DeClercq; Joanna M. Blodgett; Theou Olga; Morgan G I Langille; Robert G. Beiko

title: High-protein diet promotes aging by activating the CG6415/AMT gene and disrupting mitochondrial homeostasis
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Dietary protein has multiple physiological functions. However, high-protein diets have been proven to elevate the risk of all-cause mortality. Aging is a dynamic and complex process, but the impact of dietary protein on aging remains unclear. OBJECTIVES: To explore the effects of high-protein diets on aging at multiple life stages and the underlying mechanisms. METHODS: Drosophila were used to assess the effects of diets with 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, and 30% protein energy supply on lifespan. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses at multiple life-stage points screened pathways and key genes consistently affected by high-protein diets. Knockout and overexpression of the key gene CG6415 in Drosophila verified its mediating role in high-protein diets' impact on aging. Based on the insights from the omics data of gene-knockout Drosophila, the mechanism by which the human homologous AMT gene of CG6415 affects aging was verified in the mammalian genetic background using the human embryonic kidney 293T cell. According to the effects of high-protein diets on Drosophila's amino acid profiles, lifespan observations with individual supplementation of 20 amino acids, and verification using CG6415 gene-knockout Drosophila, the amino acids that play key roles in the impact of high-protein diets on aging were identified. RESULTS: There is an inverted U-shaped relationship between lifespan and dietary protein energy ranging from 5% to 30%. Glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism pathway and the CG6415 gene can be activated by high-protein diets of various proportions at multiple life-stage points. The CG6415/AMT gene inhibits oxidative phosphorylation, disrupts mitochondrial homeostasis, and subsequently activates the p53-p21 pathway, promoting aging and stress-induced damage. Supplementing isoleucine can partially simulate the role of high-protein diets in regulating CG6415-mediated aging. CONCLUSIONS: High-protein diet promotes aging, partly via activation of the CG6415/AMT gene and subsequent disruption of mitochondrial homeostasis. Isoleucine plays a relatively key role in this process.
authors: Xiaoqing Xu; Wangyang Zheng; Qianmin Liu; Yue Li; Shuo Yang; Runyi Zhou; Yina Wang; Xiang Qi; Can Zhang; Feng‐Min Zhang; Yue Wu; Yuhao Li; Ying Li

title: Enhancing In Vitro Fertilization Outcomes in Advanced Maternal Age
abstract: INTRODUCTION Enhancing in vitro fertilization (IVF) outcomes for women of advanced maternal age (AMA) is a significant focus in reproductive medicine. While the primary challenge is the age-related decline in oocyte quality and quantity, various strategies and adjunctive therapies have been studied to improve success rates. It is important to note that the effectiveness of these strategies can vary and what works for one person may not work for another. A personalized approach, guided by a fertility specialist, is important. Based on the references to relevant studies and research, there are some of the key strategies and treatments as below: CORE CHALLENGES OF ADVANCED MATERNAL AGE AND TRENDS IN TAIWAN Taiwan exhibits one of the most drastic trends of delayed childbearing globally. The mean maternal age at first birth has steadily increased, from 28.0 years (early 2000s) to over 32 years in recent years. The proportion of births to women aged 35 years or older has sharply risen, exceeding 30% of all births. Taiwan has one of the world’s lowest total fertility rates, consistently below 1.3 and reaching a historical low of around 0.97 in 2021.[1] Taiwan became an aged society in 2018 and is projected to become a “super-aged society” soon. IVF success rates in Taiwan, like worldwide, show a stark decline with age, highlighting the physiological challenge. Live birth rate per embryo transfer (ET) for women <35 years is around 50%. Live birth rate per ET for women more than 40 years is about 18.7%.[2] The Taiwanese government has implemented significant pronatalist policies to combat the low birth rate, with a focus on supporting IVF. Since 2021, the government offers substantial financial subsidies for IVF treatments, available to all infertile married couples where the wife is under 45 years old. The number of subsidized attempts is higher for women under 39 (up to 6 attempts) than for those 40–44 (up to 3 attempts). These subsidies encourage single ET (SET) by tying higher success rates to the number of embryos transferred, aiming to reduce the multiple birth rate associated with IVF. THE STRATEGIES TO TREAT ADVANCED MATERNAL AGE ININ VITRO FERTILIZATION–PRE-IN VITRO FERTILIZATION ASSESSMENT The baseline assessment is introduced including measuring anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), antral follicle count, and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH).[3] To evaluate the appearance of ovary, fallopian tube, and uterus and to assess the partner semen analysis. These data from the baseline assessment will guide the protocol choice and prognosis.[4,5] Based on the pre-IVF assessment, several strategic decisions are made. With reduced ovarian reserve, need more aggressive stimulation; but also balance with risk. Furthermore, choosing protocols (Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonist vs. agonist) tailored.[6] Since competence declines, more oocytes gives better chances; cumulative live birth rate (fresh + frozen ETs [FETs]) depends on number retrieved.[6] If reserve is low, do not delay. Furthermore, preemptive fertility preservation (oocyte or embryo cryopreservation) if age getting high or before treatments that might further reduce fertility. If many embryos, to select euploid ones, reduce miscarriage, improve implantation efficiency. Blastocyst biopsy and comprehensive chromosome screening seems to give better results than older methods.[7] THE STRATEGIES TO TREAT ADVANCED MATERNAL AGE ININ VITRO FERTILIZATION – OVARIAN STIMULATION Enhancing IVF outcomes for women of AMA through ovarian stimulation is a key area of research. While no strategy can reverse the biological effects of aging on egg quality, certain protocols and adjuvant therapies aim to maximize the number and quality of retrieved eggs. Traditional IVF protocols use high doses of gonadotropins to stimulate the growth of as many follicles as possible. However, in women with a diminished ovarian reserve, a common issue with AMA, this approach may not yield better results and can increase the risk of side effects.[8,9] A growing body of evidence suggests that mild stimulation protocols, which use lower doses of hormones, may be just as effective as conventional protocols for women with poor ovarian reserve, leading to similar pregnancy rates. These protocols are often associated with less cost and discomfort for the patient.[10] Use higher starting doses for those with reduced reserve or known poor responders, however, avoiding exceeding doses that are unlikely to yield benefit. Literature suggests that beyond certain FSH/luteinizing hormone (LH) daily dose thresholds (often 300–375 IU FSH + ~75–150 IU LH) may be diminishing returns.[6] Use LH activity (either recombinant LH or human menopausal gonadotropin) especially in cycles where AMH is low or previous responses have been poor. Recombinant human luteinizing hormone (r-hLH) improves oocyte yield and pregnancy rates in AMA and hypo-responders.[6] The rationale of adding LH are boosting FSH sensitivity by upregulates FSH receptors in granulosa cells,[11] supporting estrogen synthesis and follicle growth by stimulating androgen production[6] and improving follicular environment and oocyte quality, especially in aging ovaries.[11] THE STRATEGIES TO TREAT ADVANCED MATERNAL AGE ININ VITRO FERTILIZATION – LABORATORY To understand which interventions may help, it is useful to review what goes wrong in older oocytes/embryos including increased aneuploidy rates (meiotic errors and spindle defects),[6] mitochondrial dysfunction, reduced mitochondrial number or quality,[12] oxidative stress and reactive oxygen species damage,[12] slower or abnormal embryo morphokinetics,[13] and reduced ovarian reserve (fewer available oocytes/embryos).[14] Given these challenges, the goal in the laboratory is to maximize the quality of what is available: Better selection, better culture, minimizing damage, maybe some rescue/augmentation. Extended embryo culture to blastocyst stage is a strategy often employed in AMA. This allows for a more rigorous natural selection process, as chromosomally abnormal embryos are less likely to progress to the blastocyst stage. This can decrease the number of ineffective ETs.[15] Screening embryos (blastocyst stage trophectoderm biopsy and comprehensive chromosome screening) to select euploid embryos. This reduces miscarriage, improves implantation for older women whose embryo pool has high aneuploidy.[7] Maintaining optimal air quality by controlling volatile organic compounds, microbes, and chemically active compounds using high-efficiency filtration systems (like high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) and activated carbon filters, sometimes combined with advanced purification systems) has been shown to improve overall IVF outcomes, which is critical for the often more fragile embryos from AMA patients.[15] Continuous monitoring of embryo development can provide additional noninvasive data on embryo viability (morphokinetics). While early parameters may not be unique to AMA, observing developmental arrest (which is more common in AMA) can aid in selection.[13] Experimental strategies such as supplementing mitochondria (donor or autologous), spindle transfer, and pronuclear transfer are applied to try to overcome cytoplasmic/mitochondrial deficits or defective meiotic spindle function in older oocytes.[6] However, these experimental strategies as future strategies mean that AMA in IVF is still a challenge. THE STRATEGIES TO TREAT ADVANCED MATERNAL AGE ININ VITRO FERTILIZATION – FROZEN VERSUS FRESH The choice between fresh and FET to enhance IVF outcomes in women of AMA is complex, with research offering mixed findings and suggesting that the best approach often depends on individual patient factors. The factors for supporting FET include the rationale for FET is that the ovarian stimulation drugs used to retrieve eggs can create supraphysiologic hormone levels that may negatively affect the endometrial receptivity. Freezing allows a delay until the uterine lining is prepared in a more natural or hormonally optimized cycle[16] and some studies indicate that FET may be associated with a lower risk of preterm birth and low birth weight compared to fresh ET,[17] and allowing preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy (PGT-A) to screen embryos for chromosomal abnormalities (aneuploidy), which are much more common in AMA. PGT-A requires the embryos to be biopsied and then frozen while awaiting results, making FET a necessary step. Using chromosomally normal (euploid) embryos significantly increases implantation and live birth rates and decreases miscarriage rates, especially in AMA patients.[18] THE STRATEGIES TO TREAT ADVANCED MATERNAL AGE ININ VITRO FERTILIZATION – PREIMPLANTATION GENETIC TESTING UTILIZATION PGT-A is a key strategy used to enhance IVF outcomes, particularly in AMA women, generally considered to be 35 years or older. The primary benefit of PGT-A in this demographic stems from the high rate of chromosomal abnormalities (aneuploidy) in embryos, which significantly increases with maternal age.[18] By using PGT-A, IVF outcomes are enhanced by identifying euploid embryos. PGT-A screens embryos for the correct number of chromosomes (euploid). Since the risk of aneuploidy rises significantly with age (from about 25% under age 35 years to potentially over 75% past age 40 years),[18] PGT-A allows clinicians to prioritize the transfer of only chromosomally normal embryos. Transferring a euploid embryo significantly increases the chance of successful implantation, as chromosomal abnormalities are a leading cause of implantation failure. Studies suggest that when a euploid embryo is transferred, the pregnancy success rate is often similar to that of younger women.[19] By avoiding the transfer of aneuploid embryos, which would likely fail, PGT-A can reduce the number of unsuccessful cycles, leading to a faster path to a live birth.[18] The majority of miscarriages, especially in older women, are caused by embryonic aneuploidy. By transferring a euploid embryo, PGT-A has been shown to significantly reduce the risk of miscarriage compared to transferring an untested embryo.[19] PGT-A helps to reduce the risk of conceiving a baby with a genetic condition due to a chromosomal abnormality (e.g., Down syndrome and Trisomy 18) that is more common in offspring of older mothers. With the confidence that an embryo is chromosomally normal, PGT-A encourages the practice of transferring only one embryo (elective SET), which minimizes the risk of multiple pregnancies (twins and triplets), a major health risk for both the mother and the babies. However, even though PGT-A has benefits, especially in AMA, it is not magic. There are only a few cells (often from trophectoderm) in a biopsy samples. The embryo might have a mix of normal and abnormal cells. Some embryos labeled aneuploid or mosaic may still lead to healthy pregnancies. False positives can lead to discarding viable embryos. Because many embryos will be tested and found abnormal or mosaic, the absolute number of embryos you can transfer may decrease. PGT-A adds cost, lab work, possibly cryopreservation, and time. It may mean waiting until results are ready or freezing embryos until transfer. If few embryos develop to blastocyst stage, or if embryo quality is poor, PGT-A might not improve chances per retrieval; it helps more per transfer of euploid embryo. Deciding what to do with “non-viable” embryos, mosaic ones, etc., can have emotional cost. Some may worry about discarding embryos. However, PGT-A is most helpful when we have several embryos to choose from. If there are very few embryos (e.g., only 1–2 blastocysts) in AMA, testing them may not improve your chance of a baby – and could even prevent a transfer if they are tested abnormal. We might alternatively consider transferring the best-quality embryo directly instead of PGT-A. Therefore, the suggestion for AMA with few embryos is that PGT-A could be discussed as an optional tool to avoid transferring aneuploidy embryos, but only if the patient accepts the possibility of no transfer. If embryos are good quality and patient wants every chance for transfer, the fresh or frozen transfer without PGT-A is often favored. THE STRATEGIES TO TREAT ADVANCED MATERNAL AGE ININ VITRO FERTILIZATION – LUTEAL PHASE SUPPORT Progesterone is the foundation of luteal phase support (LPS); adequacy of serum progesterone matters for clinical outcomes. When luteal function is further compromised (e.g., after GnRH-agonist trigger, poor ovarian response (POR) common in AMA), consider modified LPS (higher or combined progesterone routes, earlier start, or luteal adjuvants such as low-dose human chorionic gonadotropin [hCG] or GnRH-agonist boluses).[20] Individualized serum progesterone measurement during the luteal phase (and on day of ET in hormone replacement therapy [HRT]/FET cycles) and adjust route/dose if levels are suboptimal.[21] Use a reliable progesterone route (vaginal micronized progesterone is commonly used and effective). If concern for absorption or prior low serum P, add or use an alternative/combined route (intramuscular (IM) or subcutaneous [SC] progesterone). SC progesterone is an evidence-supported alternative to IM/vaginal routes.[22] Studies show low serum progesterone on the day of ET (or in the mid-luteal phase) is associated with worse outcomes; a commonly cited threshold in HRT/FET cycles is 10 ng/mL (study-dependent). Monitoring allows dose/route adjustment.[21] GnRH antagonist protocol commonly causes luteolysis; therefore, options to rescue the luteal phase include intensive steroid supplementation or giving low-dose hCG (or dual trigger strategies). In AMA patients where embryo numbers are already low, pick a luteal rescue that preserves pregnancy chances. Because AMA patients often have poorer embryo competence, minimizing endometrial/luteal failure is critical. Therefore, some opinions suggest that starting LPS early (oocyte pick-up evening), using a robust route or dual routes (vaginal + SC/IM) and continue LPS until fetal cardiac activity (or 8–12 weeks in some practices).[22] Evidence for prolonged duration is not definitive, but clinicians often extend support in AMA. Small randomized controlled trials (RCTs)/series show potential benefit of adding GnRH-agonist boluses in GnRH antagonist cycles or low-dose hCG as luteal rescue after GnRHa trigger – but these have heterogeneity considerations. Estradiol addition has mixed evidence. Therefore, applying adjuvants for LPS should be used selectively such as prior luteal insufficiency, repeated implantation failure, or GnRHa triggering.[23] THE STRATEGIES TO TREAT ADVANCED MATERNAL AGE ININ VITRO FERTILIZATION – FUTURE PERSPECTIVES The most promising future strategies for treating AMA in IVF focus on addressing the two primary age-related challenges: Low oocyte quantity (ovarian reserve) and poor oocyte quality (aneuploidy). We make clearer separation of what is experimental/early stage and clinically applicable in the near future. THE CLINICALLY APPLICABLE IN THE NEAR FUTURE Mitochondrial dysfunction and mtDNA defects accumulate with age and impair oocyte energy metabolism; replenishing mitochondria or improving mitochondrial function may raise oocyte/embryo competence. Heterologous mitochondrial replacement techniques (spindle transfer and pronuclear transfer), autologous mitochondrial enrichment or transfer, and small-molecule mitochondrial enhancers are being reported in small series,[24-26] but results are mixed and ethically regulated in many countries. Awakening dormant primordial follicles or improving the intra-ovarian niche could increase follicle recruitment in women with diminished reserve. Intra-ovarian platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injections, drug-based or “drug-free” in vitro activation (IVA) of ovarian tissue with autotransplantation, and surgical activation techniques have been reported in small studies.[27-30] Growing number of observational studies and meta-analyses suggest that PRP may improve ovarian markers and occasional pregnancy in POR/primary ovarian insufficiency patients, IVA has produced case reports/series of pregnancies, still early and heterogeneous; randomized data are limited. The better embryo selection that nondestructively identifies embryos with highest implantation potential (and/or euploidy) could improve live births per transfer in AMA. Deep-learning models on time-lapse imaging, combined morphology metabolomics, cell-free DNA from spent media (non-invasive PGT), and AI clinical data fusion will be applied to address the goal.[31,32] The promising trials and commercial tools showing improved predictive accuracy; noninvasive PGT and AI models are under validation and will likely refine embryo prioritization. Implantation is a function of both embryo and endometrium; AMA may affect endometrial function in ways that can be personalized. Transcriptomic receptivity assays (endometrial receptivity array), single-cell endometrial profiling, microbiome modulation, individualized luteal support (progesterone monitoring and tailoring) have grown evidence that personalizing timing and hormonal support can help some patients,[33,34] however, these still show variable results and need more RCT studies. THE EXPERIMENTAL/EARLY-STAGE APPROACHES The derive eggs from pluripotent stem cells to bypass age-related oocyte decline. The preclinical progress in animals and early human cell work has been addressed with remaining major scientific, safety, and ethical hurdles before clinical use.[35] This is a true long-term prospect (years–decades). Restoring the supporting niche (stromal/endothelial) could improve follicular microenvironment by applying mesenchymal stem cell infusion into ovaries, exosome therapies, and tissue engineering approaches in some early clinical trials/case series, but biological plausibility exists. The robust clinical evidence still limited.[36] AMA is the multifactorial issue. Systematic approaches combined with multimodal interventions including metabolic assessment, mitochondrial adjustment, embryo selection, and endometrial personalization may identify synergistic protocols for AMA IVF treatment in future. Summary The challenges of AMA in IVF primarily revolve around the decline in both oocyte quantity (ovarian reserve) and oocyte quality (increased aneuploidy rates). Successful strategies to enhance IVF outcomes in AMA focus on maximizing egg retrieval and ensuring the transfer of a chromosomally normal embryo into an optimally prepared uterus. Here is a concise summary of strategies to enhance IVF outcomes in AMA, integrating current evidence and future perspectives. title: Glycine ameliorates aging-related dysfunctions associated with Nmdmc-mediated mitochondrial one-carbon metabolism
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Aging is characterized by the progressive decline of physiological integrity, and its driving factors include mitochondrial dysfunction, epigenetic changes and metabolic imbalance. Although some studies have shown that glycine (Gly) has anti-aging protection, its mechanism has not been clarified. OBJECTIVES: The purpose of this study is to explore the mechanism of Gly in anti-aging and improving aging-related phenotype, and to clarify the molecular pathway of Gly promoting healthy aging. METHODS: Fruit fly and aged rat models were used to evaluate the effect of Gly supplementation. Life span, stress resistance and functional phenotype were evaluated in fruit flies, and biochemical, histological and physiological indexes related to aging were detected in aged rats. Transcriptomic and metabolomic profiling, along with gene knockdown approaches, were used to identify key pathways and targets involved in Gly-mediated effects. RESULTS: In fruit flies, Gly extended lifespan and ameliorating aging-related phenotypes, with Gly dose-dependently upregulated the expression of Nmdmc, whose knockdown abolished these beneficial effects, indicating the essential role of Nmdmc in Gly-mediated activation of one-carbon metabolism (OCM). Metabolomic identified glyceric acid as a key metabolite linked to improved mitochondrial energy metabolism. In aged rats, Gly also upregulated Mthfd2 (the mammalian ortholog of Nmdmc) and reduced neuronal damage in the hippocampus, restored hepatic cell architecture, and increased muscle fiber density, accompanied by enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and methylation markers. CONCLUSION: Gly supplementation alleviated aging-related dysfunction by up-regulating Nmdmc and remodeling mitochondrial OCM, which could help to improve DNA repair, mitochondrial function and oxidative stress resistance.

title: Multiomics analysis reveals that senescent CXCL16+ macrophages promote lung adenocarcinoma progression through TGF-β signalling
abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is the most common histological subtype of lung cancer and remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Although, immunotherapy has become a cornerstone of first-line treatment, only 20–30% of patients achieve a durable clinical benefit, largely because of the complexity and heterogeneity of the tumour immune microenvironment. Emerging evidence indicates that cellular senescence, particularly within immune cells, contributes to tumour progression by impairing antitumour immunity; however, its mechanistic role in LUAD remains incompletely understood. We performed an integrative multiomics analysis incorporating genome-wide association studies (GWASs), bulk RNA sequencing, single-cell RNA sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics to characterize immune heterogeneity in LUAD. Cellular senescence was validated by performing staining for senescence-associated β-galactosidase and the canonical markers p16 and p21. SHAP analysis was applied to evaluate the contribution of CXCL16 + macrophages. Functional roles were assessed using coculture assays, in vitro and in vivo tumour models, orthotopic tumour implantation, and multiplex immunofluorescence staining of clinical specimens. A summary data-based on Mendelian randomization analysis integrating GWAS and TCGA data identified CXCL16 as a senescence-associated gene that is causally linked to the LUAD risk. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that CXCL16 is predominantly expressed in macrophages, and the pseudotime analysis together with β-galactosidase staining confirmed its association with macrophage senescence. Spatial transcriptomics and immunofluorescence staining showed the marked enrichment of CXCL16 + macrophages in LUAD tissues. The cell–cell communication analysis further revealed a strong association between the number of CXCL16 + macrophages and the activation of the TGF-β signalling pathway within the tumour microenvironment. Functionally, CXCL16 + macrophages promoted LUAD progression via TGF-β signalling, as validated in vitro and in subcutaneous and orthotopic tumour models. Molecular dynamics simulations additionally suggested that LUAD patients with high levels of CXCL16 + macrophage infiltration may exhibit increased sensitivity to bosutinib. CXCL16 promotes macrophage senescence, and senescent CXCL16 + macrophages drive LUAD progression through TGF-β signalling. These findings identify CXCL16 + macrophages as a biologically and therapeutically relevant immune cell population, highlighting a potential target for precision intervention in LUAD.

title: ERRα-NOS2-mediated citrulline metabolism attenuates tubular epithelial cell senescence in diabetic kidney disease
abstract: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is a leading cause of end-stage renal disease, characterized by tubular epithelial cell (TECs) senescence, inflammation, and fibrosis. This study investigates the role of estrogen-related receptor alpha (ERRα) in regulating TECs senescence in DKD through nitric oxide synthase 2 (NOS2)-mediated citrulline metabolism. We demonstrate that ERRα expression is significantly downregulated in renal tubular cells of both diabetic mice and DKD patients, correlating with increased senescence markers and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Mechanistically, transcriptome and chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing confirmed that ERRα regulates NOS2 transcription. TECs-specific knockout of ERRα led to reduced NOS2 expression and decreased citrulline levels, exacerbating TECs injury and senescence. In contrast, TECs-specific knock-in of ERRα alleviated TECs injury and senescence and restored citrulline metabolism. These findings indicate that ERRα plays a critical role in regulating NOS2-mediated citrulline metabolism, which is essential for maintaining kidney function and mitigating tubular senescence in DKD. Furthermore, overexpression of NOS2 and supplementation with citrulline ameliorated renal dysfunction and cellular senescence in diabetic mice, underscoring the importance of this metabolic axis. Modulating ERRα and NOS2 activity may present a potential therapeutic strategy to reduce kidney injury and slow the progression of DKD.
